learningObjectives: Differentiate Decision tables and Decision trees from simple When Conditions, and explain how each returns a result.
Select the appropriate Decision Rule type for a given scenario and test Decision Rules for conflicts and completeness.

elements.description: A Decision table maps tested conditions to outcomes. Each column uses its property/operator pair across rows; different columns may test different fields. The topic’s App Studio calculated-field procedure creates a Decision Table Rule in Work-, not a universal storage rule for all tables.

elements.text: Compare a grid of combinations with nested questions. A table can put several input fields in columns and combinations in rows. A tree follows conditional branches, with later questions depending on earlier ones. Either may express similar logic, but choose a readable structure supported by the consuming configuration.

elements.description: A suitably authorized Process owner can maintain a delegated table. The Results tab’s Delegation options control which editing capabilities are available, such as adding rows or columns. Those options are not by themselves a grant of user access or the entire delegation setup.

Without Evaluate all rows, processing stops at the first matching row. Enabling it checks every row; only matching rows perform their configured actions and return calculations. Consumers such as an authority matrix can collect multiple successful results; checking rows does not make every row match.

elements.term: Direct flow processing with Decision tables
elements.description: Add a Decision shape in a flow pointing to a Decision Table. Each result value maps to a flow connector, directing the Case to a different path — keeping branching logic out of the flow diagram.

elements.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 760 190" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" font-family="inherit"><title>Table combinations versus nested branches</title><rect x="10" y="10" width="740" height="170" rx="12" fill="var(--pa-surface)" stroke="var(--pa-brand)"/><text x="30" y="42" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="var(--pa-brand)">Table combinations versus nested branches</text><text x="30" y="74" font-size="14" fill="var(--pa-ink-2)">Table: each column tests its configured input across the rows.</text><text x="30" y="104" font-size="14" fill="var(--pa-ink-2)">Tree: a matching parent condition can lead to a child comparison.</text><text x="30" y="134" font-size="14" fill="var(--pa-ink-2)">Choose readable logic and check support in the consuming configuration.</text></svg>
elements.caption: A table can test multiple properties in separate columns. A tree can use nested conditions; neither representation is automatically interchangeable in every consuming configuration.

elements.description: Handles logic that returns a result from test Conditions. Each branch evaluates a property/operator pair against a single value; a true comparison can lead to nested branches. Decision trees can test DIFFERENT properties and operators across branches.

A branch combines a comparison and an action: return a result, continue or stop evaluation. A matching parent can lead to child comparisons. Otherwise supplies the fallback when evaluation does not return a result.

elements.term: Where Decision trees can be referenced
elements.description: Decision trees (and Decision tables) can be referenced in:

elements.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 760 190" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" font-family="inherit"><title>Nested conditions and review</title><rect x="10" y="10" width="740" height="170" rx="12" fill="var(--pa-surface)" stroke="var(--pa-brand)"/><text x="30" y="42" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="var(--pa-brand)">Nested conditions and review</text><text x="30" y="74" font-size="14" fill="var(--pa-ink-2)">A parent comparison must match before its nested question is evaluated.</text><text x="30" y="104" font-size="14" fill="var(--pa-ink-2)">Returning a result differs from continuing to another comparison.</text><text x="30" y="134" font-size="14" fill="var(--pa-ink-2)">Check conflicts and completeness; a clean check is not business validation.</text></svg>
elements.caption: The tree’s branch structure controls which comparisons run. Delegation editing options are described for Decision tables; do not generalize their tab location to trees.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Choosing: Decision Tree vs. Decision Table

elements.term: When to use a Decision table
elements.description: Prefer a table for many combinations of the same set of properties. A column uses a consistent property/operator pair; other columns can use other inputs. The table is not restricted to one field.

elements.term: When to use a Decision tree
elements.description: Prefer a tree when branch-specific questions depend on prior conditions. Different branches may use different inputs or operators. This is a structural preference, not proof that any multi-field decision requires a tree.

Show conflicts identifies conditions made unreachable by other rows or branches, such as an earlier broad match shadowing a later narrower one. An unreachable row may still have satisfiable conditions in isolation. Evaluate all rows removes that first-match shadowing check, not every possible logic error.

Identifies missing conditions in a Decision table or missing branches in a Decision tree. 'Show completeness' can generate a LARGE number of rows for many-valued combinations; the user determines which suggested conditions are necessary.

examPitfalls.title: Same pair per column, not one property per table
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Multiple columns can test a shared set of input fields across combinations. Do not infer that different properties always require a Decision tree.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Use a table for combinations and a tree for conditional nesting; check the consuming feature’s support.

examPitfalls.title: 'Evaluate all rows' disables 'Allowed to return values'
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Candidates know 'Evaluate all rows' returns multiple results but forget the side effect on the 'Allowed to return values' setting.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: When 'Evaluate all rows' = true, the 'Allowed to return values' setting is automatically DISABLED. These two options are mutually exclusive.

examPitfalls.title: Conflict test shows NO conflicts when 'Evaluate all rows' is on
examPitfalls.trapDescription: With Evaluate all rows, earlier matching rows do not stop later evaluation. The reviewed conflict check consequently does not report that first-match shadowing. This does not prove the conditions are satisfiable or the business outcomes are correct.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Every row is checked, but only matching rows perform their configured action. Validate meaningful test cases even when no conflicts are reported.

examPitfalls.title: Conflicts are warnings, not errors — they appear on Guardrails landing page
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A question asks what happens when a Decision Table has a conflict and the app is run. Candidates say 'a runtime error is thrown.' Conflicts appear as Guardrail warnings — the application still runs, but the conflict is flagged on the Guardrails landing page.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Conflicts are reported as WARNING messages when you save the Decision Rule form and displayed on the Guardrails landing page. They don't prevent saving.

examPitfalls.title: Assignment routing via Decision table updates Assign-Workbasket class
examPitfalls.trapDescription: The source’s Work Queue routing example notes an update to Assign-Workbasket. It does not require every routing Decision Table to be defined in that class.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Distinguish the Assignment-routing class update from the Decision Table’s own Applies To class.

examPitfalls.title: Decision trees can be nested — a true result leads to another comparison
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A tree supports a later question conditional on an earlier match. A table can also express multiple conditions; nesting is a readability/configuration choice rather than a restriction on table capabilities.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Decision tree branches can be nested. A 'true' result on one branch triggers evaluation of a child branch for additional comparisons — allowing complex multi-level logic.

examPitfalls.title: Delegation editing options do not grant access
examPitfalls.trapDescription: For an already delegated table, Results-tab Delegation options control editing capabilities. Granting stakeholder access and selecting editable features are different steps.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Set up authorized delegation, then control the permitted edits with the table’s Delegation options.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A logistics manager already has authorized access to a delegated Decision table. Where does a developer control whether the manager may add rows or columns while maintaining it?

options.text: Configure Delegation options in the Decision table’s Results tab to control permitted editing capabilities
Enable 'Evaluate all rows' in the Results tab so all threshold rows are always processed
Move the Decision table to the Data- class so non-developer users can access it
Add the logistics manager as a co-owner of the Decision table Rule in Dev Studio

practiceQuiz.hint: Which specific configuration option delegates Rule maintenance to stakeholders?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Results-tab Delegation options control the features available when maintaining an already delegated table. They are not the whole user-access setup; evaluation mode and class placement do not substitute for editing capabilities.

optionExplanations.A: These options restrict edits offered to an authorized delegate; they do not themselves grant all access to a previously inaccessible Rule.
optionExplanations.B: Evaluation mode controls processing of matching rows, not whether a delegate is permitted to add columns or rows.
optionExplanations.C: Class placement is not the control for permitted delegated editing features; changing it may also change applicability.
optionExplanations.D: Rule co-ownership is not the table editing-options section described by the source for an authorized delegate.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An approval authority matrix must collect every applicable approver from one Decision table: manager above $500 and VP above $1000. Which evaluation setting lets both matching rows contribute?

options.text: Select 'Evaluate all rows' in the Results tab of the Decision table
Create two separate Decision tables — one per approval level — and chain them in the flow
Add a When Condition to each row to explicitly allow both to fire simultaneously
Use a Decision tree instead — Decision tables can only return one result

practiceQuiz.hint: What setting makes a Decision table return all matching rows instead of the first match?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Evaluate all rows checks each row and performs the configured action for each match, allowing the authority matrix to collect applicable approvers. The approval workflow must still consume those results; nonmatching rows do not fire.

optionExplanations.A: Checking every row allows each matching approver entry to contribute; the consuming authority matrix handles the collected results.
optionExplanations.B: Separate tables can model separate logic, but they do not answer which setting enables multiple matches within this one table.
optionExplanations.C: Per-row conditions determine whether a row matches; the table evaluation mode controls whether processing stops after the first match.
optionExplanations.D: The claimed one-result-only restriction is false because the source describes all-successful-result processing for tables.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A developer enables 'Evaluate all rows' on a Decision table. What happens to the 'Allowed to return values' setting?

options.text: It is automatically disabled — the two settings are mutually exclusive
It expands to show a larger list of allowed values since more rows can fire
It is moved to the Delegation options section of the Results tab
Nothing — 'Allowed to return values' operates independently of 'Evaluate all rows'

practiceQuiz.hint: What is the explicit side effect of enabling 'Evaluate all rows' on the Results tab?
practiceQuiz.rationale: When 'Evaluate all rows' = true, 'Allowed to return values' is automatically DISABLED. The settings are mutually exclusive. B, C, and D all describe behaviors that do not occur.

optionExplanations.A: The reviewed Rule form disables Allowed to return values when Evaluate all rows is true; this is the described setting interaction.
optionExplanations.B: A larger allowed-value list is not the stated effect; the source explicitly describes disabling the setting.
optionExplanations.C: The setting is not relocated into Delegation options; the described effect is disabling it under this evaluation mode.
optionExplanations.D: Independence contradicts the source note that enabling all-row evaluation disables Allowed to return values.

practiceQuiz.scenario: In the reviewed Work Queue routing procedure, which Assignment class does the source note is updated in Dev Studio?

options.text: The Assign-Workbasket class Rule is updated in Dev Studio
The Assign-Worklist class Rule is updated in Dev Studio
The Flow Rule is updated to include a Work Queue router step
A new Decision Rule of type Router is created in the application ruleset

practiceQuiz.hint: Which specific class Rule is updated when routing an Assignment to a Work Queue via a Decision table?
practiceQuiz.rationale: The source notes an Assign-Workbasket class update for Work Queue routing. This is not a requirement that the routing Decision Table itself must use that Applies To class, or proof that no Flow configuration changes occur.

optionExplanations.A: Assign-Workbasket is the class named in the reviewed Work Queue routing note, not a mandatory class for every routing table.
optionExplanations.B: Assign-Worklist is not the class named for the Work Queue routing example; individual-user routing is a different target.
optionExplanations.C: This option does not identify the Assignment class asked about; do not infer that no Flow configuration can also change.
optionExplanations.D: The source does not introduce a new Decision Rule type named Router; it describes selection of a Decision table router.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A Decision tree evaluates a job candidate. Branch 1 asks 'Years of experience > 5?' — if true, Branch 2 asks 'Has required certification?' — if true, returns 'Eligible for offer'. What Decision tree feature does this demonstrate?

options.text: Nested branches — a true result on one branch triggers evaluation of a child branch
Evaluate all rows — both conditions fire simultaneously regardless of the first result
Conflict detection — the two branches are checked against each other for overlap
Completeness testing — the tree checks all possible value combinations automatically

practiceQuiz.hint: What is it called when a true Decision tree result leads to another comparison?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Nested branches allow a true result on one condition to trigger a child branch for further evaluation. This is a key structural feature of Decision trees. B is wrong — 'Evaluate all rows' is a Decision table feature. C and D describe testing features, not the structural evaluation pattern.

optionExplanations.A: The second comparison depends on the first match; this is the nested branch structure described for a Decision tree.
optionExplanations.B: The two comparisons are not unconditional simultaneous row matches; the second is nested under the first branch.
optionExplanations.C: Conflict testing examines unreachable conditions; it does not name this parent-child evaluation structure.
optionExplanations.D: Completeness testing examines missing coverage rather than the configured nesting that controls these two comparisons.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Customer tier equals Bronze, Silver or Gold, with a result for each. Which representation is preferable for a concise grid of the same property/operator comparisons?

options.text: Decision table — all conditions test the same property/operator pair ('Customer tier =')
Decision tree — multiple branches allow the property to be tested for all three values separately
Decision tree — Decision tables cannot handle more than two distinct values in a column
Neither — tier categories can only be evaluated by an Activity

practiceQuiz.hint: When all conditions test the SAME property/operator pair, which rule type is preferred?
practiceQuiz.rationale: The table is a concise fit for these repeated category comparisons. A tree could express them, but the question asks for the grid preference, not exclusive technical capability.

optionExplanations.A: A table compactly represents repeated tier equality comparisons; the question asks for that readable grid preference.
optionExplanations.B: A tree could express the logic, but it does not provide the requested compact grid of repeated property comparisons.
optionExplanations.C: The two-value limit is invented; a table column can compare more than two configured category values.
optionExplanations.D: An Activity is not required merely because tier has categories; the table approach directly models this mapping.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A decision asks about certification only on the experienced-candidate branch, and about training eligibility only on the inexperienced branch. Which representation most directly shows this dependent hierarchy?

options.text: Decision tree — each branch can lead to its own conditional questions
Decision table — all branch-dependent comparisons must always share one condition column
When Condition — it can return all named eligibility outcomes rather than a true/false result
Decision table — Evaluate all rows automatically creates parent-child branch nesting

practiceQuiz.hint: Which rule type is preferred when conditions evaluate different properties and different operators?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Nested tree branches directly show which later comparison depends on the earlier outcome. Multi-column tables remain valid for combinations of properties; they are not technically restricted to one field.

optionExplanations.A: Branch-specific follow-up questions naturally form a hierarchy, matching the structure requested rather than an exclusive capability rule.
optionExplanations.B: Tables can use multiple columns; the claimed mandatory single-column restriction is incorrect and does not model the requested nesting.
optionExplanations.C: A When Rule answers true/false rather than returning all the named eligibility outcomes requested here.
optionExplanations.D: All-row evaluation controls table matches; it does not automatically generate the parent-child branches of a tree.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which TWO locations are explicitly listed as references for both Decision tables and Decision trees in the reviewed comparison topic?

options.text: Flow Rules
Declare Expressions
A Ruleset version’s locking field
An Operator password field

practiceQuiz.hint: Decision tables and trees can be referenced in Flow Rules, Declare Expressions, activities, and routers.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The comparison topic lists Flow Rules, Declare Expressions, activities and routers. The two offered members of that list are A and B; this is not a claim that calculated UI fields cannot indirectly use Decision logic.

optionExplanations.A: Flow Rules are explicitly listed for referencing either decision structure, subject to the configured decision consumer’s support.
optionExplanations.B: Declare Expressions are explicitly listed as a location for referencing either decision structure in the comparison topic.
optionExplanations.C: A locking field controls Ruleset modification; it is not one of the explicitly listed decision invocation contexts.
optionExplanations.D: An Operator password field is an authentication concern, not a listed Rule context for invoking these decision structures.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A developer runs 'Show conflicts' on a Decision table that has 'Evaluate all rows' enabled. The test reports no conflicts. Why?

options.text: Checking all rows removes first-match shadowing from this conflict check; it does not certify every condition or result
The conflict test only works on Decision trees, not Decision tables
The Decision table has no overlapping conditions, which is why no conflicts are found
Conflicts require at least 5 rows to be detected — the table has fewer rows

practiceQuiz.hint: Why does 'Evaluate all rows' change what the conflict test can find?
practiceQuiz.rationale: The source says the conflict check reports none with Evaluate all rows because evaluation is not stopped by an earlier match. Nonmatching or impossible conditions and incorrect business results still require review.

optionExplanations.A: All-row evaluation removes the early-stop shadowing examined by this check; other logic defects can still remain.
optionExplanations.B: The reviewed conflict tools apply to both tables and trees, so limiting them to trees is incorrect.
optionExplanations.C: No reported conflicts under this mode does not prove there is no overlap; the mode changes the check’s reachability behavior.
optionExplanations.D: A minimum-five-row requirement is not described; the effect here follows from evaluation mode rather than table size.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A developer runs 'Show completeness' on a Decision table and gets hundreds of suggested rows. What should they do?

options.text: Review the suggestions and determine which are actually necessary for the business logic — not all suggestions need to be added
Add all suggested rows — 'Show completeness' only suggests rows that are required by the application
Disable 'Evaluate all rows' first — completeness can only generate accurate results when single-result mode is on
Split the Decision table into multiple smaller tables — large tables cannot pass completeness testing

practiceQuiz.hint: 'Show completeness' can generate many rows — who decides if they're needed?
practiceQuiz.rationale: The user determines if the suggested conditions from the completeness test are actually necessary. 'Show completeness' can generate a large number of rows when there are many combinations — not all suggestions are required.

optionExplanations.A: A developer must decide which suggested combinations matter; the completeness check cannot infer every business requirement.
optionExplanations.B: Suggested rows are not automatically mandatory business rules; blindly adding them may create unintended outcomes.
optionExplanations.C: The topic does not require disabling all-row evaluation before reviewing completeness suggestions as this option claims.
optionExplanations.D: Many suggestions reflect combinations, not proof that a table must be split or cannot be tested.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A developer saves a Decision table and sees warning messages about conflicting rows. Where else are these conflicts visible?

options.text: On the Guardrails landing page
In the Dev Studio error log under System Management
In the Case Lifecycle view as a guardrail violation badge
In the App Studio validation panel when the Case Type is next opened

practiceQuiz.hint: Besides the save message, where do conflict warnings appear?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Conflicts are reported as warning messages when saving the Decision Rule form and are displayed on the Guardrails landing page. B, C, and D describe locations that are not mentioned in Pega Academy for Decision Rule conflict visibility.

optionExplanations.A: The source identifies Guardrails as another place for Decision conflict warnings reported when saving the Rule form.
optionExplanations.B: A system error log is not the warning visibility location identified in this reviewed procedure.
optionExplanations.C: The source does not identify the Case Life Cycle badge as the additional location for these saved Decision conflict warnings.
optionExplanations.D: An App Studio validation panel is not the additional conflict-warning location described by this source.

practiceQuiz.scenario: In Dev Studio, a developer needs to add a Decision shape to a flow to direct Case processing based on a Decision Rule result. Where do they find the Decision shape?

options.text: Flow shapes > Decision
Automation shapes > Evaluate
Case shapes > Branch
Rules panel > Decision Rules > Add to flow

practiceQuiz.hint: What is the navigation path for adding a Decision shape to a flow in Dev Studio?
practiceQuiz.rationale: The reviewed Dev Studio procedure uses Flow shapes → Decision. This identifies that documented route rather than asserting that no other authoring interface can expose an equivalent task.

optionExplanations.A: This is the reviewed Dev Studio path for selecting a Decision shape before specifying its decision logic.
optionExplanations.B: The topic does not use this Evaluate entry under Automation shapes for the requested Decision addition.
optionExplanations.C: The documented task is not a Branch entry under Case shapes; follow the reviewed Flow shapes procedure.
optionExplanations.D: This Rules-panel route is not the documented shape-addition procedure requested by the scenario.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An SA is choosing between a Decision table and a Decision tree for a new rule. Which TWO statements correctly differentiate Decision trees from Decision tables in Pega?

options.text: Decision trees support hierarchical branches where a condition can lead to a more-specific child comparison
Decision tables evaluate multiple conditions across columns in a row-based format where all columns in a row must match
Decision trees are restricted to Boolean true/false outputs and cannot return text or numeric results
Decision tables can only contain a single condition column and return a single binary output

practiceQuiz.hint: Tables can combine columns; trees can nest questions. Match the structure to the consumer and result.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Trees support nested questions, while tables organize combinations across columns and rows. The result must suit its consumer; neither structure is restricted to Boolean output, and neither universally supports every possible data type.

optionExplanations.A: A child question can depend on a parent condition; not every branch must have a child or use a different property.
optionExplanations.B: A table row can combine several condition columns and return its result when the configured combination matches.
optionExplanations.C: A Decision tree is not confined to Boolean results; the reviewed examples return named outcomes such as approval eligibility.
optionExplanations.D: A table can contain several input columns and nonbinary outcomes; the one-column binary-only restriction is incorrect.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A developer runs a conflict check on a Decision table and finds issues. Which TWO statements correctly describe how Pega handles Decision Rule conflicts and gaps?

options.text: Show conflicts can identify a later row made unreachable by an earlier broader match in first-match evaluation
The Rule form’s Show conflicts and Show completeness tools help inspect unreachable conditions and missing coverage
Pega automatically resolves Decision table conflicts by selecting the matching row with the highest row number
Decision tree conflicts are impossible by design because each branch always produces a unique, non-overlapping result

practiceQuiz.hint: Distinguish unreachable conditions from mere overlap; use the Rule form’s named checks.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The conflict test checks whether conditions are prevented from being used; the completeness tool suggests missing coverage. Partial overlap alone does not establish an unreachable row, and neither tool automatically supplies correct business logic.

optionExplanations.A: An earlier broad match can shadow a later narrower row under first-match processing; that is the source’s conflict example.
optionExplanations.B: These named Rule-form checks examine reachability and missing combinations, with business review still needed afterward.
optionExplanations.C: The source’s first-match behavior is not automatic selection of the highest numbered row to resolve conflicts.
optionExplanations.D: Trees can have shadowed branches too; nesting does not guarantee every branch is reachable or nonoverlapping.

quickRecap.value: Each column keeps its configured property/operator pair across rows. Multiple columns are supported. Evaluate all rows checks all rows; matches perform actions.
Branches can test different inputs and lead to nested questions, return a result or continue. Otherwise provides a fallback.
Prefer a table for combinations of a repeated input set, a tree for dependent branch questions; check consumer support.
The source Work Queue routing example updates Assign-Workbasket; this does not set a universal Applies To requirement for routing tables.
Check shadowed rows/branches. Evaluate all rows changes the conflict check, not the truth of every condition. Warnings also appear on Guardrails.
Finds missing conditions/branches. Can generate many rows. User decides which suggestions are actually needed.
Authorized delegation allows stakeholder maintenance; Results-tab Delegation options control the available table editing features.
